And there's no place that I can see that it says deacons, therefore, managing the household of God, too. It's just a qualification, a good preparation. It's what makes them qualified for their job. So I hate to jump from the fact that they are supposed to be managers of their home to necessarily saying that, therefore, they should be managers in the household of God, because then they really are junior ruling elders, and I think they lose their calling. And this is the way most people treat, what do you think people treat deacons as? They treat them as junior elders, people with potential. So we kind of put them on probation, even though it explicitly says in 1 Timothy 3.12, these should be not new men, but men who have already been tested. And Calvin at one point says, I can almost quote him, I can't say this word for word, he says this difference between elders and deacons is not one of maturity, but one of calling. I say it shouldn't be that deacons are less mature guys. They should have a different basic calling and function. So I'm a little bit afraid of just mixing them on up. But, you know, maybe Dick's right. That's an awful thing to say after I just argued against it. Yeah, Rod, then I'll move over here. So would you say that there's a difference in quality Is there a difference between the ordination of a deacon and the ordination of an elder? Well, oh yeah, I think so. As far as authority is concerned. See, I really think we could probably have other ordained, we could ordain other kinds of people and workers in the church. You know, it's very hard to find a word. There is no one word for ordain. There's no technical word for ordain. You do a study of that. There's no technical word either in Greek or Hebrew. There's a whole family of words that talk about appoint or elect or pick out. And I believe that there's only two permanent offices in the church. I'm not sure that we have to distinguish them by having them be the only ones that we ordain people to. Sound too radical to you? So in other words, the argument that you were saying as far as just because you lay hands and ordained a deacon doesn't give them authority over you. You do not apply that argument to elders. No, you couldn't say that. Well, you see, you ordain a person to use their gift. The gift of an elder, in order to discharge his gift, he has to have authority over you. So when you're ordaining him, you're just ordaining him, you're recognizing him and setting him apart to exercise his gift, and you give him the freedom to use that gift in the church, and in order to do that, you give him authority over you. When you give the deacon freedom to use his gift, you don't give him authority. See, my idea of ordination is you publicly recognize a person, give him freedom to use the gift in the midst. That's the essence that all ordinations have in common. The ruling elder gets authority simply because of his gift. But the argument that is on the other side of the fence for me is anyone who gets ordained gets authority automatically by virtue of the ordination. A kind of ex operae operatum thing. As soon as I lay hands on you, you've got authority. I'm not sure that that's true. But... Could be wrong. Yes, Dave, and then Bob. It seems to me that both Dr. Gaffin's analogy of the family life and the church life and the question of authority, if you really look at the authority structure of a home and a family, the woman has a special place of authority. It's an odd place. Because she's over authority of the children. Over the children. I mean, in my household, she's in charge of spending money. She is in most every household. She certainly... All kinds of delegated authority. Right, all kinds of delegated authority. There's a lot of stuff that's going on, and it's authority too, and not authority over. She is not an authority over me. A wife should not be an authority over her husband. Now... Dr. Daffin seemed to be putting the office of deacon and the office of elder in a parallel structure, which sounds more like Christian reform, but you've got to appreciate the fact that it is a different calling to a different office, which has a different question of authority. Yeah, so you're arguing along the lines of my own thinking. Though I must say that in order to get across the idea of ordination, having inherently authority being invested when you ordain somebody. in the British Presbyterian churches, that is the UPUSA, PCUSA, PCAOPC, you'll usually find that in the vows, even though deacons are not part of the consistory, and they don't take part in those kinds of things, you'll find in the vows, we promise to give you as a deacon all the honor and obedience to your office. Like in the PCA it says, we promise to give you all the honor and obedience to your office. And frankly, if I... Women shouldn't be deacons if that's the vow that you take. And I'm not sure how in the world I obey the deacons anyway, frankly. I've given them the freedom to represent me and exercise decision-making power, but I just don't see what... I mean, I think Craig's right. They've got authority over something I've given them, but they don't have authority over me. Okay, I've got to go to Bob and then David. I guess I've got some awfully fundamental confusion. I think it comes in two forms. One is, I didn't really understand it as a matter of sort of delegated authority or given authority when the hands were laid on the deacons. I thought this was the identification of the deacon having become one of the congregation of Greece who exercised the authority of Christ in the ministry. to which he's called. And in that authority, it would seem to me that the authority that he exercises is not with respect to you, unless you are the need in need of mercy. In which case, the recipient of mercy, it seems to me, does come under the authority of the one who is rendering it. Well... In that case, it really is delegated, though, because if I don't like the way the deacons are handling it, I immediately ask the elders, and deacons are only, even though the elders give the deacons freedom. Well, that may be the way it works, but is it not true, kind of as a matter of principle, that those who are to receive mercy do come in a certain sense of the authority of those who are rendering it on behalf of the... congregation. Yeah, I think there's something to that. Well, in that case, isn't there an issue of male or female co-ordinated relations? That would be the argument on the other side of the fence, yeah. There's weight to that argument. Though I'm trying to go one step further. To really be consistent, you better not have anybody teaching any classes who are not elders or deacons. Because there's no way that you come any more under the authority, say, of a deacon who's helping you out than you come under the authority of your small group leader or your teacher or that sort of thing. In a certain sense, they are telling you what to do. They're giving you assignments. They're leading you and saying, here's things that you need to do to get yourself together. It's the same thing with deacons. Deacons come. They give you money. They tell you, here's what we want you to do to get yourself together. We'll help you get a job and so on. I think in that sense, yeah, they are. You know, you have some kind of discipling, a deacon has some kind of discipling leadership over you, but it's not, it doesn't have any teeth to it, it's not disciplinary authority of the elders of God. But I would say that if you're going to say that deacons have authority over people, because they're officers and they have authority, if you're going to define authority like that, you better be very careful in a sense that... that all sorts of folks in the church that are dealing with people and leading them and bringing them along, they would be officers as well. If you say, well, you don't have to be an officer to be a Sunday school teacher because they don't access any authority, I think they're access to the same amount of authority that deacons are. I'm making my case. You know, Bob, I mean, you've got weight to what you're saying. I'm not saying that it's a silly thing. Now, wait a minute. David hasn't had a chance. Go ahead. I was unable to grasp the final... It is fine. Oh, Romans 16. First, David, why don't I concede to Dick and say that that is an exegetical standoff. It is a hard thing to prove one way or the other, and as far as I'm concerned, pull it out, and you could still have a real good old-fashioned scrap. You could have a good old-fashioned scrap and argue both the ways we're arguing without Romans 16. He does agree that it's a title. That it was some kind of position, not just a general statement saying, well, she has done a lot of good things. He won't grant that it was the office of deacon. And you know, he may be right. That's the reason that I can't press on that. I still think the most likely thing is that deacon, as if Phoebe was whatever verse 11 was talking about. And that Phoebe and the women in verse 11 were probably the same thing that the Order of Widows was talking about. Yeah, and I can live with anybody who decides that because of the placement, we can call these women deacons and ordain them, as long as they understand that that doesn't mean they give them any disciplinary authority over the church and men. And I can live with that, or I can live with the people who say that we need to have an unordained, appointed body of women. Call them what you want to, because actually the name deaconesses is not in the Bible, but it's the women. Well, whatever you want to call them, you should have an order of women who work in mercy and so on. I'm very happy with that. I'm not real happy with not making any provision. at all, for women being recognized as being workers in mercy that are working with the deacons. I'm not very sympathetic with that. That's where most of our churches are, at least in the Reformed churches. Now we can round two. Alan? I was just with Craig and I were talking about what Bob's concern was. If you had women deacons, would you turn it over again? Let's say you had someone who, as Paul said to him, doesn't want to provide him for his household. and the deacons have been providing assistance. He's the head of household. Ah, yes. Isn't that discipline? Yeah, well, see, no, because you really, if a person who's a member of the church, you're helping them out, and the Bible says, he who does not work shall not eat. So here's a person who, after a lot of exhortation and talking and so on, you can see that he's just being irresponsible. The deacons shouldn't cut things off unless the elders are involved because that's a very serious sin. He's sinning against his household. The elders need to be involved to admonish the man not working, not providing for his household. They should be involved. I don't think you should do that without the elders being involved with it. So I don't think the deacons... Well, they work in tandem. They'd work in 10. I don't think the deacons should just pull out, especially now if it's a member. Now, it depends. If you're talking about a non-member, the evangelism team has met a person in the community who's got a lot of economic needs and they're sharing the gospel with them. The guy starts to come to church. He's got some needs. The deacons work hand-in-hand with the evangelism team to start to help the man out while the evangelism team is seeking to lead him to Christ. That's very, very, very valid. You're over here in this. This little block, okay? Now, what happens if after a while he's just showing an unwillingness to really be responsible with the money or that kind of thing? I don't believe at that point, obviously, deacons can cut him off, but that's not discipline of any sort. And they had no authority over him anyway. In a lot of cases, there's a lot of times where deacons do work with people who are not members of the church, who are not Christians, as part of an outreach to them. And at a certain point, they just refuse to come around, and then they should be cut off. And that's not disciplinary authority. Although I would certainly say that deacons are something that needs to be going for now. Otherwise, we're totally neglected to get some money. Yeah, thanks. I'm not in the camp of people who are adamant just because I do believe in unity. You're too adamant, you know. I could be wrong about things. You don't want to be adamant when you're just virtually sure of yourself and you don't mind fracturing things. And I don't want to do that. Any other questions on this? I mean, I thought there were more hands than I got to. Did somebody maybe have your questions answered, right, by somebody else? Yeah, Barry. Yeah, I'll get to that. Certainly that's a type of theatrical work. Oh, it's diakonia, too. It says. That's what they did. It uses the Greek word, too. They did it. They were doing diakonia with the apostles. inherent in the actual work that is authoritative, it cannot be supported by that pastor because that's certainly the actual type of work to Christ. It doesn't prove much, unfortunately, though it does prove that in a sort of a prototype of the church, you have, here's Jesus, the teaching elder, and you have the apostles, and then you've got the women who are the deacons. I mean, it's sort of a, but it doesn't prove anything. I'm not saying that that's necessarily... I don't think there is. And now, what we're going to do, probably the last half of the next hour, the hour on Friday, I'm going to try to show you, see, and this is very important too, I'm going to try to show you that there historically have been three... approaches to what is the primary purpose of the deacon. The one approach, which actually comes from the Roman Catholic Church, is that the main job of the deacon is administrative assistance. The deacons were secretaries to the bishop and administrative assistance. And there are people, that's J.F.'s viewpoint. I'm not trying to call him Roman Catholic. You read in Pastoral Leadership, his book on Shepherding God's Flock, you'll read a section where he says the main job of the deacons is to take off the administrative details off of the pastors and the ministers so that they are freed up to do the ministry of the word. And that's, by the way, I want you to know that there's a lot to that. The second basic approach is the approach that comes to us from the Church of Scotland, and that is deacons were financial officers. That was their primary thing. The primary thing was they got the money and distributed it, because you've got to remember the parishes in the Church of Scotland, each parish not only ran the church and paid the minister, but ran the schools, and basically the whole social structure of the community came together through the deacons, and the deacons were the financial officers, and that was their main job. In other words, the idea of the deacons were trustees. They got the money, they took care of the money, they took care of the profit, trusteeship. is the main thing deacons do. That's the second basic approach. The third basic approach is that deacons are primarily ministers of mercy. They take care of people with hurts and needs. And that comes to us from the continental churches. It comes to us mainly from the Dutch Reformed churches. That says that's the primary purpose of the deaconate. And I think all three of those things are valid. But you see, to some degree, there's some division of labor. Deacons are supposed to be doing all three of those things. And that actually has some bearing on women as deacons. Just like what Calvin did was he said, okay, the trustees, administrators are one kind of deacon, and the mercy work with cases is another kind of deacon. And he basically said one kind of deacon, males are... eligible for that job and for the other ones, both men and women. So we're going to talk more about that. And if you use the word diaconal work to mean mercy ministry, which we'll define again next time, I really don't see any reason why women couldn't be deacons. If you use the word diaconal ministry to define more than that, in many ways, women shouldn't be. So, you see, if somebody says to you, should women be deacons? You should say, it all depends. So...

For all other information, please visit the main website at www.wts.edu. We're going to be talking about both the General Office of Believer Lay Ministry and the Office of Deacon, or Deaconal Ministry. Let me put it this way. The next three weeks, we're going to be...

talking about the forgotten blocks in Edmund Clowney's Rubik's Cube. Now, let me explain. You remember Edmund Clowney's Rubik's Cube of the church. It looks something like this. Now, I practiced before I came in here to see if I could draw a pyramid, a three-dimensional pyramid, and I failed. So it really didn't make any difference. It's something like this, right? Now watch. Oh, not bad so far. Now, this has to be a little longer.

Okay. Oh, that's out too far. Oh, well. What do you think? Now, wait a minute. Is it my imagination? There's only three sides. Oh, there's four sides. If you all remember, from the Living in Christ Church, Ed Clowney, down here at the bottom, you know, he's got this...

divided like this. And let me give you a, oh boy, it's really getting worse all the time. Let me give you a picture of his diagram of the ministry of the church. And this down here is the bottom. The bottom of the pyramid has got these nine categories. He says the ministry of the church, the objects of the ministry of the church are, of course, God, that's our ministry to God, our ministry to the saints,

and our ministry to the world. That's worship and edification and witness. That's the goals of ministry. Or, as Dr. Conley likes to say it, you can really reduce everything that the church does, all the ministries of the church, you can reduce it to singing. Because, you see, worship is just singing God's praises to God, and edification is just singing God's praises to each other.

And witness is what? Singing God's graces to the world. So everything comes down to singing. So those of you who can't carry a tune, work on it. And that's what worship and edification and witness is. But Ed Clowney also graphs against that the three functions. And the three functions of ministry are the word, the ministry of the word, the ministry of order, and the ministry of mercy.

or, as has often been called, the prophetic ministry, taking the word of God and speaking the word of God to people. The priestly ministry is where you are representing people to God. The prophetic ministry is where you're representing God to people, you see. The prophetic ministry, taking the word. The priestly ministry, which is mediating, you might say,

the relationship between God and man. And then you have the, whoops, I blew it, the priesthood ministry is the ministry of mercy, right? Yeah, you're right. And this is the kingly ministry, which is the ministry of order or discipline or government. And in the traditional understanding of the Presbyterian church, this is the pastor or the teaching elder, this is the governor or the ruling elder, and this is the deacon.

Now, remember, this is just the bottom of the pyramid. The reason it's good to graph these things against each other, and you should have read about this in the little book, Living Christ Church, which you all read the first week, right? Of course, absolutely. Some of your noses are growing longer, but that's okay.

For example, the reason that Ed Clowney grafts these against each other is, look, very carefully. There's a tendency sometimes to talk about, well, you have the functions of worship, and you have edification, and you have witness, and then you have mercy, and then you have preaching. Ed Clowney is very wise in realizing these are grafted against each other. For example,

Deeds of mercy, compassion to people in need. And we're going to talk about that at some length in the next couple of days. Deeds of mercy or compassion are a witness to the world. That is, they go along with our evangelism, their way of ministering to people. So, you see, deeds of mercy are a witness. In a certain sense, when the world sees us meeting...

When the world sees our ministry of the Word, and it sees people's lives being changed, coming to church saying, my marriage has put together, my life has been put together, the world scratches its head because it can't figure it out. It looks like sleight of hand, you know, it looks like the emperor's new clothes or something. They'll turn in the same preacher that you said has changed your life. They'll listen to the guy and they'll say, I don't get it.

It's boring to me. But when the world sees us feeding people who are hungry and dealing with people who are in need, the world can see us do that. That doesn't look like sleight of hand. Deeds of mercy are very much a witness. Deeds of mercy are very much a part of fellowship. Fellowship, you know, koinonia, means to share. And, of course, sharing means we share everything we've got with each other, not just our quiet times, but also our pocketbook. That's part of fellowship, okay?

And then, of course, obviously deeds of mercy are a pleasing sacrifice to God, as stated many, many times. So you see, these things all graph against one another. Now, in the same way, for example, edification, to really fill up the saints, takes mercy, you see, it takes preaching the Word of God, and it also takes discipline and order and discipling, you see, and it takes shepherding.

Now, when I talk about the forgotten blocks in this cube, this Rubik's Cube, you realize again that Ed Clowney divides the pyramid and says, down here you've got the general office of believer, up here you've got the special offices, and at the top, of course, you've got...

Jesus Christ the Mediator, who is a prophet, priest, and king. The teaching of Reformed Ecclesiology historically has been that every believer has got to be doing all of these things at the level of what Reformed Ecclesiology is always called the level of the general office of believer. That means the Bible calls every believer to be a prophet, a priest, and a king, and every believer to worship and to build up the saints and to witness the world. Every believer.

But then, at this level, there's specific offices that major on certain areas of this. So there's specific offices that ministers of the Word who major on the preaching of the Word, and there's officers who major on ministry of mercy, and there's officers who major on discipline and order. And in a certain sense, one of the jobs, you can say, of the minister of the Word is not just to minister the Word.

but also to be equipping all the people down here in this part of the pyramid so that they are doing what the Bible calls every believer to do. Every believer is supposed to minister to the Word. How? Every believer is to witness. Every believer is to teach. Every believer is to exhort. Exhort one another daily, lest you be hearted by the deceitfulness of sin. Let the Word of God dwell in you originally so you can teach and admonish one another. That's in Colossians 3.16. Every believer is supposed to have the Word of God dwelling in them and ministering the Word.

It's also true that every believer, so every believer is a prophet. One of the most astonishing, some of you heard me say this over, lately I've been getting into, I've been meditating on this one verse, so it keeps popping up when I speak. It's in Matthew 11, when after Jesus has talked to the messenger from John the Baptist, telling him why he's the Messiah.

He turns around and says something about John the Baptist, and he says, when you go out to see John the Baptist, what do you go out to see? A prophet? He says, yes, and more than a prophet. He says, I tell you that among those born of women, and that is a pretty big group, among those born of women, there is not one greater.

been born than John the Baptist. He's the greatest prophet up to now. And then he turns around and says, and I say to you, the least in the kingdom of God is what? Greater than he. Now that can't mean that the least in the kingdom of God, that the least Christian in the church is necessarily more godly, prays more. I happen to know, at least in my own part, that that's not true. I don't know about you.

But he's talking about the prophetic office, you see. He's saying that the least believer has got it all over the Old Testament prophets. It doesn't mean that every believer is necessarily getting objective public revelation, but it means that the revelation we've got is so much more full than what John the Baptist had. It means the anointing. You see, all of us have spiritual gifts. The anointing of the Spirit is the sort of thing that Moses called for back in the book of Numbers. I think it's in chapter 11. He says, oh, I wish that all...

of God's people could prophesy. And then we're told in Joel that in the Messianic time, all God's people would be prophets because the Spirit would fall on them. And then in Acts 1, we're actually told. Peter tells us. What happened at Pentecost? All of God's people now are prophets because the Spirit has fallen. All God's people are prophets. All God's people are priests.

We're told in Hebrews, we're told in the book of Hebrews that all of us have access, you see, through the high priest, Jesus Christ, to the presence of God. And we're also told, another thing that the priests did besides bring people into the presence of God, they also did deeds of mercy. It was the priests and the Levites who took care of the poor. You gave your alms to the priests and the Levites. They dealt with the poor.

In fact, they were the public health officials. Why do you think that when Jesus would heal a leper, he'd tell the man to go stir yourself to the priest? Why? You know, just to stir up trouble? No. Because the priest was the public health officer of the community. The priest had to declare him clean. The priests were the social workers.

In the book of Hebrews, we see again and again, we're told we're all priests because we have a high priest. We all have access to the throne room of God, and we're all supposed to be sharing what we have and doing deeds of mercy because those are pleasing sacrifices. We're told that in Hebrews 13. Share what you have and do deeds of mercy. And therefore, you see, every believer is a priest.

In fact, the idea that every believer is a priest means that, number one, that all believers are supposed to be doing deeds of mercy. Number two, it means all believers can participate in worship. That's one thing you get out of 1 Corinthians 12 and 14. What's interesting, when it says, and we'll get to this maybe later, when it talks about women being sure that they have their heads covered, that they show they're under authority.

when they're praying and prophesying and worship. You see, there's no question that all believers are priests, that everybody comes and has a hymn and has a psalm and has something to share. The question is, we have to make sure that women are demonstrating, Paul is saying, we have to make sure women are demonstrating that in the household of faith that there is that order. Nevertheless, all believers are priests. Why? All believers take part in worship. Why?

Because they're all priests. Because they have access to the throne of God. We don't have the same problem they had in the Old Testament. Only the priests could go approaching God. Everybody else had to sort of stay still and hope they didn't get zapped. Now, all believers are kings. We're told very specifically, Revelation 1, we're already kings and priests. 1 Peter 2.9, you're already a what kind of priesthood?

Royal. You're already kings. And that means, and this is the hardest one to figure out, it means every believer is a king. Now, there's some churches when it's pretty obvious everybody knows that. And the way in which they exercise that is that nobody listens to the leaders. But there's also a tremendous danger.

There's a tremendous danger of getting across the idea that you guys have got out there, all these believers, you've got to submit to the authority of the elders and lose back to the fact that all believers are kings. It certainly means a couple of things. It means all believers have authority over the world, the flesh, and the devil. Romans 6, you have authority over the flesh, you have authority over the devil.

You know, greater is he who is within you than he who is out there in the world. You know, the place in 1 John that says, this is the triumph. You know, here's the victory that overcomes the world. That's our faith. Every believer's got authority over the world, the flesh, and the devil. And every believer's a king. Now, traditionally, say, for example, in Reformed Ecclesiology, that has meant that believers have the right to choose their officers.

You see, if you would say that believers don't have the right to elect their officers in a certain sense, you're de-kingifying them. You'd have to say that. But I think we can even go further than that. And I'm going to share with you in a minute some people who believe that in the name of good order, we are telling believers they can't take initiative in ministry. They have to wait for us to ask them to do something.

If it means anything to say all believers are kings, it means that believers are allowed to take the initiative in ministry and to organize and do it certainly in coordination with everyone else under the guidance of their officers. But another way to put this, and nobody can quite track it down, when we say all believers are prophets, priests, and kings, another way to put this in sort of modern lingo, every believer is a messenger, a minister, and a manager.

We haven't been able to track down where that came from. It's just sort of a modern way to put it. Every believer is a prophet, a priest, and a king. Every believer is a messenger, a minister, and a manager. Well, a manager, you hear that? Every believer is a manager. That doesn't mean that in the church that believers are all errand runners. You see, if I am delegating, there's two ways in which I can delegate something to you if I'm in charge. One of the things I can say is you can research.

what I'm asking you to do. You can research it. You can look into it. You can recommend, but you have to come back to me. You can't make a move unless I approve it, basically, unless I tell you what to do. The other way in which I can delegate a job to you is I can say, here's your job, go about it, make the decisions, do it, and report to me. I have the right to overrule. I have the right to say you're out of line, but report to me. Those are two different ways to delegate, right? In one case, you could not call that person the manager.

No way. He's really, you know, he's an executive secretary, but he's not a manager. In the other case, you're delegating to a person in such a way that you're letting him be a manager. If we're saying that every believer is a messenger, a minister, and a manager, every believer is a king, I think we have to recognize that we have to find ways of making sure the laity really understands that we want them to minister, and they're not supposed to sit around waiting for us to call them up and ask them to teach Sunday school or something else like that.
Now, before going on, I guess I should say, couldn't catch me there, could you, John? Bet you didn't get me. Before I go on, I probably should answer your question. Yeah, right.

the offices of the work that's done on these offices, the right side. I understand the three levels of the pyramid, but I don't understand how the vertical that God and saints in the world ties into the athletic office. Oh, okay, sure. I did it down here. For example, mercy ministry is a ministry to the world because we are supposed to be doing deeds of mercy.

as we evangelize people. So, for example, when I... Just plain old-fashioned friendship evangelism usually starts by helping somebody out. Hospitality is mercy ministry. Taking them in, feeding them, that kind of thing. Ministering the Word to them. So mercy ministry is ministry to the world. Mercy ministry is ministry to the saints. Mercy ministry is honoring to God. When you offer your alms, John Calvin believed...
